sources.title: Lynch, Ross, and Crowley: Pacific Languages, an Introduction
sources.note: Open scholarly synthesis of Pacific language histories, diversity, contact, and the limits of broad Papuan classification.

sources.title: ANU Press: Uncovering Pacific Pasts, chapter 34
sources.note: History of New Guinea archaeology, highland sequences, changing interpretations, and the difference between evidence and inherited models.

sources.title: Papua New Guinea Flexible Open and Distance Education: Grade 7 Social Science
sources.note: Government education text locating the early Portuguese encounter on western New Guinea and describing exchange rather than conquest.

sources.title: Gaffney and colleagues: Earliest Pottery on New Guinea Mainland
sources.note: Peer reviewed Wanelek evidence for highland pottery, coastal and inland manufacture, polished axes, and long-distance influences.

sources.title: David and colleagues: Keveoki 1 and hiri ceramics
sources.note: Peer reviewed archaeological record for a short-lived Gulf village and ceramics around 450 to 500 calibrated years BP.

sources.title: Irwin, Shaw, and McAlister: Origins of the Kula Ring
sources.note: Peer reviewed regional synthesis of Massim pottery, exchange, seasonal winds, canoe performance, and late prehistoric change.

sources.title: Shaw and colleagues: Village-specific Kula partnerships
sources.note: Peer reviewed obsidian sourcing showing northern Massim connections by 1350 to 1500 and distinct village histories.

sources.title: David and colleagues: Ruisasi 1 mass-produced ceramics
sources.note: Open peer reviewed Caution Bay evidence for standardized vessels, a pottery midden, marine specialization, and an earlier regional network.

sources.title: ANU Press: Kuk Swamp artefacts and Phase 5 houses
sources.note: Archaeological chapter dating sparse Phase 5 houses near 1500, garden drainage, food preparation tools, and sampling limits.

sources.title: ANU Press: Kuk Swamp houses and settlement
sources.note: Archaeological and later ethnographic comparison of house forms, family use, rebuilding, pigs, and the danger of simple back-projection.

sources.title: ANU Press: Archaeologies of Island Melanesia, technological process
sources.note: Archaeological and ethnographic study of pottery production, materials, makers, exchange, and technological process around Madang.

sources.title: Lilley: Prehistoric exchange in the Vitiaz Strait
sources.note: ANU thesis on pottery, obsidian, shell, bone, food remains, and exchange linking New Guinea with the Bismarck Archipelago.

sources.title: Irwin: Emergence of Mailu as a central place
sources.note: ANU archaeological study of settlement spacing, environmental zones, pottery manufacture, clay sources, and trade in coastal Papua.

sources.title: Shaw and Dickinson: Excavation on Nimowa Island
sources.note: Peer reviewed late prehistoric settlement, pottery, shell, stone, burial, exchange, and decorative continuity in the Louisiades.

sources.title: Rethinking agency in hiri exchange relationships
sources.note: Peer reviewed synthesis centering Gulf oral traditions, inter-family partnerships, temporary adoption, sago, pottery, and chronological limits.

sources.title: Hardy and colleagues: Ceramic analysis and oral traditions
sources.note: ANU research combining Gadsup and Agarabi oral histories with ceramic chemistry to reconstruct local movements and exchange.

sources.title: Writing New Guinea Languages: Alphabets and Orthographies
sources.note: Linguistic study stating that Motu received its first developed orthography and school publication in 1877.

sources.title: ANU Press: Pre-contact encounters and linguistic responses
sources.note: Scholarly account of multilingual Pacific trade, Papuan and Austronesian contact, and trade-language development.

sources.title: Tropical Foodways and Exchange along Northeastern New Guinea
sources.note: Peer reviewed last-millennium evidence from shell, animal remains, dental calculus, and pottery residues around Madang.

sources.title: Piperno: Microfossil perspectives on human-plant interaction
sources.note: Peer reviewed synthesis of Kuk starch and phytolith evidence for ancient banana, taro, cultivation, and preservation limits.

sources.title: Denham: Evidential basis for early pigs and pottery in Melanesia
sources.note: Peer reviewed reassessment showing that pig and pottery chronologies in New Guinea require source criticism and new dates.

sources.title: Papua New Guinea Medical Journal: South-coast bioarchaeology
sources.note: Medical journal abstract comparing oral disease and childhood stress at late prehistoric Nebira and Motupore.

sources.title: Australian Museum: Learning process in highland stone tools
sources.note: Museum account of observed tool manufacture, teaching, raw material choice, and the chronological limits of ethnographic analogy.

sources.title: Koch and colleagues: East Sepik medicinal plant survey
sources.note: Community and university-linked modern survey showing locally varied plants, preparations, uses, and incomplete clinical validation.

sources.title: UNESCO: Cultural Landscapes of the Pacific
sources.note: UNESCO study of Kuk drainage, cultivation, pigs, exchange, landscape history, and the need to avoid one linear agricultural story.

sources.title: Australian Museum: New Britain stone-tool geochemistry
sources.note: Museum-published geochemical study tracing flaked and ground tools through intra-island and inter-island movement.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.name: Papua New Guinea
proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas label for diverse eastern New Guinea communities, not one polity.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact missing record is papua-new-guinea, indexed once with the alias Papua N Guin from 1492 to 1530.
The imported modern state name is treated as a regional umbrella, not a sixteenth-century polity, people, language family, or fixed cultural unit.
All fifty border snapshots were audited; two exact features occur in two files and have two decoded hashes but the same shape counts and tested memberships.
The target includes selected central and eastern mainland probes but excludes many northern, southeastern, island, western, and Torres Strait probes.
The 1530 papuans-1530 feature is broader, while the 1715 papua-new-guinea-1715 record inherits a later reduced shape; neither is associated to this card.
Eight teaching periods cover every year from 1492 to 1530 without treating their artificial internal boundaries as local events.
Local archaeological ranges and later oral or ethnographic evidence are dated and bounded rather than generalized across the atlas polygon.
No secure community-authored written-language sample for the exact polygon and interval was found; later orthographies and outsider texts are not substituted.
The 1530 endpoint is an atlas relabeling and continuity, with fell null and no predecessor or successor association.
